newsitem.title: ITALY: We were victims, fashion gurus tell Italian trial.
newsitem.headline: We were victims, fashion gurus tell Italian trial.

text.p: Two of Italy's top fashion names told their bribery trial on Wednesday that the payments had been extorted from them by greedy tax inspectors.
Versace fashion house chairman Santo Versace and designer Krizia are among seven defendants on trial in the same case.
Both testified that they had paid tax officials during inspections in 1990 but said they were forced to hand over the money. Prosecutors allege the money was paid for easy audits.
"I feel I am the injured party here," said Versace, brother of designer Gianni Versace. He added he had finally agreed to pay 300 million lire ($190,000).
He said inspectors turned up in January 1990 and made it known that they wanted one billion lire to leave "otherwise they would stay there to eat the Christmas cake".

"I am an accountant and I think that to do a complete audit takes no more than a week if you want to work. Instead, we realised that they were there to occupy the business, perhaps because there were beautiful girls around," he said.
"They were effectively stopping us from working."
Krizia, whose real name is Mariuccia Mandelli, said tax inspectors who audited her company in March 1990 had asked for 250 million to 300 million lire.
"Our internal administrator told me after a while that the inspectors were making absurd notes but they were writing everything down in pencil and you can rub out pencil," she said.
Krizia said she had signed a written contract to pay over $260,000 through foreign accounts.

"I thought this document could come in useful...Instead I found myself under investigation. Now, when I go abroad, I'm always asked in interviews how the trial is going. I will fight to the finish against this charge," she said.

Several other top fashion names charged with the same offence, including style guru Giorgio Armani, bowed out of the trial last year after paying damages and receiving suspended sentences under plea-bargaining arrangements, which in Italy do not require guilty pleas.
Armani said he wanted to close a chapter that was upsetting him professionally but did not consider himself guilty.
The trial was adjourned after Wednesday's testimony until February 21.
